title: Kimchi Fried Rice
summary: Day-old rice fried hard with sour, well-fermented kimchi and its juice, finished with a fried egg. The best use for the half jar at the back of your fridge and the rice you forgot about yesterday.

ingredients.name: cooked short-grain rice
ingredients.notes: Fresh rice steams instead of frying; spread it on a plate to dry if you have no leftovers

ingredients.name: napa cabbage kimchi
ingredients.notes: The sourer and older, the better

ingredients.name: kimchi juice
ingredients.notes: squeezed or poured from the jar

ingredients.name: scallion
ingredients.preparation: white and green parts sliced separately

steps.instruction: Break up the cold rice with wet hands so there are no clumps. Chop the kimchi and squeeze its juice into a small bowl; keep the juice.
success_cues: Rice is loose and grainy with no fist-sized lumps
About 3 tablespoons of red juice collected
steps.creator_note: Cold rice is the whole trick here. Warm, fresh rice turns to mush the moment it meets the kimchi juice.

steps.instruction: Heat the oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat. If using spam or bacon, fry it now until the edges crisp, then add the scallion whites and garlic and stir for 30 seconds.
success_cues: Meat edges are browned and crisp
Garlic smells toasty but is not brown
warnings: Garlic burns in seconds at this heat; keep it moving and lower the flame if it darkens.

steps.instruction: Add the chopped kimchi and the gochujang (if using). Fry, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until the kimchi darkens and the pan smells sweet and sour.
success_cues: Kimchi turns a deeper red and the sharp raw smell softens
Liquid in the pan has mostly cooked off

steps.instruction: Add the rice, kimchi juice and soy sauce. Press the rice flat against the pan with the back of a spatula, leave it alone for a minute, then toss. Repeat two or three times.
success_cues: You hear a crackle when the rice sits still and some grains turn crisp
steps.creator_note: Pressing and waiting is how you get the crispy bits. Constant stirring gives you soft rice.

steps.instruction: Turn off the heat. Stir in the sesame oil and most of the scallion greens. Taste and add a little more kimchi juice or soy sauce if it needs it.
success_cues: Rice tastes sour, salty and a little sweet with no raw-rice blandness

steps.instruction: In a separate small pan, fry the eggs sunny-side up in a little oil until the whites are set and the yolks are still runny.
success_cues: Whites are fully opaque with lacy brown edges
Yolk still wobbles when you nudge the pan
warnings: Runny yolks are undercooked egg; cook the yolk through for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or immunocompromised.

steps.instruction: Divide the rice between two bowls, slide an egg on top of each and finish with the remaining scallion greens, sesame seeds and crumbled seaweed.
success_cues: Yolk breaks over the rice when cut and coats the grains

creator_notes: This is a fridge-cleaning recipe: leftover roast vegetables, a handful of frozen peas or yesterday's chicken all go in at step 4.
If your kimchi is fresh and barely sour, add a teaspoon of rice vinegar with the juice to get the tang back.
dietary_warnings: Kimchi often contains fish sauce or salted shrimp; check the label for a vegetarian version. Soy sauce and gochujang usually contain wheat.
